Rabies — Foundations & Replication

Core characteristics pp. 1–3

  • Causative agent: Rabies virus.
  • Transmission: classically through the bite of an infected animal.
  • Disease pattern: rapidly progressive acute infectious disease of the CNS in humans and animals.
  • Outcome: almost always fatal.
  • Public-health importance: widespread among animal reservoirs.

Structure and genome

  • Family: Rhabdoviridae.
  • Genus: Lyssavirus.
  • Shape: rod or bullet particles, about 75 × 180 nm.
  • Envelope: present, with protruding barrel glycoprotein spikes about 10 nm long.
  • Spikes are trimers of viral glycoprotein.
  • Inside the envelope is the ribonucleocapsid.
  • Genome: nonsegmented negative-sense ssRNA, about 12 kb and 11,932 nucleotides.
  • Contains RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

Five encoded proteins

  • N — nucleocapsid protein.
  • P — phosphoprotein.
  • M — matrix protein.
  • G — glycoprotein.
  • L — large polymerase protein.
Study aidN → P → M → G → L is the gene order from the 3′ leader side toward the 5′ trailer side. This same order explains the transcription gradient later.

Reaction to physical and chemical agents p. 1

ConditionLecture statement
Survives storageAt 4°C for weeks.
At −70°C for years.
Inactivated byCO₂.
Killed byExposure to UV or sunlight.
Heat for 1 hour at 50°C.
Lipid solvents.
Trypsin.
Detergents.
Extremes of pH.

Replication sequence pp. 1–2

1. Attachment. Viral G protein binds host-cell receptors. Binding is most effective to neural cells, although receptors on other cell types such as muscle cells can also be used.
↓
2. Endocytosis and fusion. The virion enters an endosome. Fusion releases internal components into the cytoplasm. M protein dissociates from the nucleocapsid, exposing the ribonucleoprotein core.
↓
3. Primary transcription. Encapsidated RNA becomes the template. The transcriptase complex, especially RdRp, begins at the 3′ end.
↓
4. Sequential mRNA synthesis. The genome order is Leader → N → P → M → G → L → Trailer. Intergenic regions contain gene-end and gene-start signals. The intergenic nucleotides themselves are not transcribed.
↓
5. Capping, polyadenylation, and termination. Each viral mRNA is capped at initiation. At an intergenic region the polymerase receives a polyadenylation signal, adds a poly-A tail, terminates the prior mRNA, and then attempts to restart downstream.
↓
6. Transcription attenuation. Restart succeeds in about 70–80% of junction events and fails in about 20–30%. Fewer polymerases reach late genes, producing a gradient with N mRNA most abundant and L mRNA least abundant.
↓
7. Translation. Ribosomes translate the viral mRNAs. High N mRNA abundance produces high N-protein levels.
↓
8. Switch to replication. When enough N protein is available, it binds the 5′ encapsidation signal of nascent RNA. Encapsidation makes the polymerase ignore intergenic stop-start sequences and produce a full-length positive-sense antigenome.
↓
9. Genome synthesis. The antigenome trailer contains an efficient encapsidation signal. With enough N protein, a full-length encapsidated negative-sense genome identical to the original genomic sequence is produced.
↓
10. Assembly and budding. G protein is synthesized on rough-ER-bound ribosomes, moves through the ER-Golgi pathway to the plasma membrane, and forms trimers. M protein links the nucleocapsid to the cytoplasmic tails of G trimers. Budding releases progeny virions.
Key differentiator
Transcription makes individual capped and polyadenylated mRNAs.
Replication makes full-length encapsidated antigenome and genome strands.
The abundance of N-protein mRNA is intentional and supports the transcription-to-replication switch.

Rabies — Pathogenesis, Pathology & Immunity

Neuroinvasion and spread p. 3

Must know
Virus is present in large quantity in the saliva of infected animals.
Transmission is almost exclusively by inoculation of infected saliva through a bite or scratch.
Risk rises with multiple bites and inoculation into highly innervated sites such as the face and hands.
  1. After a bite, the incubation period is usually 20–90 days, but it may be only a few days or more than one year.
  2. During incubation, virus remains at or close to the inoculation site.
  3. In muscle, it binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on postsynaptic membranes at neuromuscular junctions.
  4. It spreads centripetally along peripheral nerves to the spinal cord or brainstem through retrograde fast axonal transport, up to about 250 mm/day, with roughly 12-hour delays at synapses.
  5. It enters the CNS.
  6. It rapidly disseminates through the CNS along neuroanatomic connections by fast axonal transport.
  7. Once CNS infection is established, it spreads centrifugally along sensory and autonomic nerves to salivary glands, heart, adrenal glands, and skin. In salivary glands it replicates in acinar cells and is secreted into saliva.
Key differentiatorThere is no well-documented evidence for hematogenous spread of rabies virus in the lecture.

Pathology p. 3

  • Negri body is pathognomonic.
  • Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in brain neurons.
  • They contain rabies virus proteins and viral RNA.
  • Observed in Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus.
  • Present in about 80% of cases, so they are not seen in every case.
  • Highest viral titers are in the submaxillary salivary glands.
  • Rabies virus has not been isolated from the blood of an infected person.

Infection also triggers inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, autophagy, and apoptosis to help control viral spread.

How rabies virus suppresses this response

Viral proteinLecture-described immune-evasion action
NConceals viral RNA from RIG-I, protecting it from host-defense sensing.
PInhibits ISGs and IRF3/7, reducing IFN-β and weakening interferon signaling.
MDampens innate immune gene expression. It also participates in assembly and can induce host-cell apoptosis.
GReduces T-cell activation and promotes IL-10 secretion while also mediating viral entry.
Result of suppression
Poor cytokine and chemokine response.
Limited leukocyte infiltration into the CNS.
Absent neutralizing antibodies.
Immune-cell apoptosis.

Rabies — Clinical Presentation, Diagnosis & Prevention

Clinical presentation p. 4

  • Incubation: usually 1–3 months in the clinical section.
  • Symptoms have been reported from 5 days after exposure to as long as 8 years.
  • Two acute neurologic forms are emphasized: encephalitic or furious rabies and paralytic rabies.

Prodrome

  • Nonspecific features: fever, malaise, headache, nausea, vomiting, anxiety, and agitation.
  • Earliest specific neurologic symptoms: paresthesia, pain, or pruritus near the exposure site.
  • Often presents as atypical encephalitis with relative preservation of consciousness.
Encephalitic versus paralytic rabies
FeatureEncephalitic or furiousParalytic
Proportion80%20%
Dominant pictureFever, confusion, hallucinations, combativeness, seizures.Muscle weakness with early prominent flaccid weakness.
Autonomic featuresHypersalivation, gooseflesh, cardiac arrhythmia, priapism.Sphincter involvement is common.
Classic differentiatorEarly brainstem involvement produces hydrophobia and aerophobia.Excitability and hydrophobia are absent.
CourseHyperexcitability alternates with lucid intervals that shorten as disease progresses. Brainstem dysfunction rapidly progresses to coma and death.Weakness may begin distally and spread to quadriparesis and facial weakness. Sensory involvement is mild.
Common confusion—Commonly misdiagnosed as Guillain-Barré syndrome.
OutcomeRapid progression. Aggressive management may still be complicated by cardiac and respiratory failure, arrhythmias, water-balance disturbance, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and GI hemorrhage.Usually survives a few days longer than encephalitic rabies, followed by multiple-organ failure.

Diagnostics and treatment p. 4

ApproachLecture details
Antigen or nucleic acidImmunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase uses antirabies monoclonal antibodies to detect tissue antigen.
RT-PCR can amplify rabies genome segments from fixed or unfixed brain tissue or saliva. Sequencing can identify the infecting strain.
PathologyNegri bodies in brain or spinal cord support a definitive pathologic diagnosis.
SerologySerum antibodies by IF or neutralization testing provide supportive evidence, especially later in disease.
Viral isolationHamster and mouse cell lines can be inoculated. Growth may occur within 2–4 days. Isolates are confirmed by fluorescent antibody tests.
Animal observationAnimals considered rabid or suspected rabid undergo laboratory examination. Other animals should be observed for 10 days. Animals developing encephalitis, rabies, or unusual behavior are humanely killed and tissues are examined.
Exam trapThere are no tests that diagnose rabies before clinical symptoms appear according to the lecture. Once symptoms appear, multiple laboratory tests can confirm the diagnosis.
Treatment
There is no established treatment for rabies.
Symptomatic treatment may prolong life, but outcome is almost always fatal.

Immunization and post-exposure prophylaxis pp. 4–5

Core prevention principleBecause rabies is always fatal once symptoms appear, vaccination is the cornerstone of prevention.
  • Vaccine stimulates a strong cellular immune response involving CD4 helper cells and T cells.
  • Plasmablasts and memory cells appear early and correlate with rising antibody levels.
  • Booster doses trigger faster and stronger responses and support durable protection.

Control toolbox listed in the lecture

  • Human rabies vaccine.
  • Rabies vaccines for dogs.
  • Rabies immunoglobulin.
  • Diagnostic Negri body.
  • Rabies virus culture.
  • Diagnostic fluorescent-antibody tests.

Pre-exposure prophylaxis

  • For immunologically naive individuals: 2-site ID or 1-site IM vaccine on day 0 and day 7.
  • Routine booster or serology titers are considered when continued high risk of rabies exposure remains.

Slow Virus Infections

General characteristics p. 5

  • Defined as chronic and persistent.
  • Have a long asymptomatic period with a months-to-years gap between introduction of the agent and clinical illness.
Progressive neurologic diseases in the lecture
GroupExamples
Conventional virus diseasesSubacute sclerosing panencephalitis or SSPE.
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy or PML.
Unconventional agentsKuru.
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis p. 5

  • Rare demyelinating CNS disease.
  • Associated with chronic nonpermissive measles virus infection.
  • Nonpermissive means virus is present in brain tissue but does not permit full viral replication.
  • Measles virus persists in a defective or altered form in neurons and glial cells.
  • Persistence leads to progressive inflammation, demyelination, and neuronal damage.
  • Frequency given as about 1 in 100,000–500,000 measles cases.
  • Typical history: measles at an early age, around 2 years, followed by a 6–8 year latent interval before progressive neurologic disease.
SSPE clinical progression
StageFeatures
InitialPoor school performance.

Myoclonus.
Ataxia.
Visual disturbances.
LateVisual disturbances.
Unresponsiveness.
Quadriparesis.
Spasticity.
Hyperactive tendon reflexes.
Hyperactive extensor plantar responses.

Laboratory findings

  • CSF anti-measles antibodies are invariably elevated.
  • Positive oligoclonal anti-measles antibodies.
  • Brain tissue can be cultured using cocultivation techniques.
  • Immunocytochemistry detects viral antigen.
  • In situ hybridization and PCR detect viral genome.
Treatment and prevention
No definitive therapy is available.
Vaccination is the lecture-listed preventive strategy.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy p. 5

  • Caused by JC virus of the Polyomaviridae family.
  • Occurs in immunosuppressed individuals.
  • May occur as a complication of therapeutic monoclonal antibody use.
  • Characterized by CNS demyelination from reactivation and replication of JC virus.
  • Signs and symptoms: visual deficits, mental impairment, weakness, ataxia, and seizures.
Diagnostic approachLecture finding
MRIMultifocal asymmetric, coalescing white-matter lesions in centrum semiovale, parietal and occipital regions, and cerebellum.
CSF PCRPositive PCR for JCV DNA.
Specificity 92–100%.
Sensitivity is variable.
Treatment
No consistently effective therapy is available.
Mirtazapine may inhibit JCV binding to its receptor on oligodendrocytes.

Prions

Characteristics p. 6

  • Proteinaceous infectious particle that lacks nucleic acid.
  • Composed of folded proteins that undergo self-propagation.
  • Described as epigenetically heritable.
  • Examples listed: scrapie, mad cow disease, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
  • Only known transmissible pathogens without nucleic acid.
  • May occur as infectious, genetic, or sporadic disorders.
  • Genetic disease can involve a mutation in the PRNP gene.
  • Pathogenicity results from accumulation of PrPSc derived from normal PrPC.
  • Different prion strains can have different biologic properties because they fold in slightly different ways.

Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies p. 6

  • Small size, <100 nm.
  • Incurable.
  • No nucleic acid genome.
  • Extremely resistant to heat, disinfectants, and irradiation.
  • Can be deactivated by strong chemicals such as phenol, periodate, sodium hydroxide, or sodium hypochlorite.
  • Slow replication with incubation periods that can reach 35 years or manifest late in life.
  • Cannot be cultured in vitro.
  • Do not elicit immune or inflammatory responses.
  • This silent persistence allows major brain damage before clinical recognition.
1. PrPC synthesis and transport. Synthesized through ER and Golgi, then transported to the cell surface.
↓
2. Attachment. At the plasma membrane, PrPC is attached by a glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor.
↓
3. Initiation of misfolding. Abnormal PrPSc contacts PrPC at the cell surface or in endocytic vesicles and forces a conformational change. The lecture calls this the protein-only hypothesis.
↓
4. Oligomer formation. Misfolded proteins cluster as oligomers of PrPSc. Lipid rafts and cofactors such as sulfated glycosaminoglycans or proteoglycans can make this process more efficient.
↓
5. Accumulation and deposition. PrPSc accumulates in lysosomes, plasma membrane, or extracellular space and may form amyloid fibrils and plaques.
↓
6. Consequence. Accumulation in nervous tissue produces neurodegeneration.

DiseaseLecture detail

Classic CJDGradual progressive dementia, ataxia, myoclonus, and death.
Sporadic CJDSpontaneous transformation of normal prion protein into abnormal prions.
Iatrogenic CJDContaminated growth hormone preparations.
Contaminated surgical instruments.
Cadaveric human dura mater grafts.
Host response and outcome
No inflammatory response and no immune response.
No interferon production.
No impact on B-cell and T-cell production.
The lecture also notes that chronic lymphocytic inflammation may affect prion pathogenesis, with accumulation in organs affected by chronic inflammation.
No treatment. The lecture describes prion disease as always fatal.

Human Cancer Viruses — General Concepts

General principles pp. 6–7

  • Viruses are etiologic factors in several human tumors, including cervical cancer and hepatocellular cancer.
  • The lecture estimates that 15–20% of human tumors worldwide have a viral cause, including HPV, EBV, HHV-8, hepatitis B and C, HIV, and HTLV.
  • Tumor viruses frequently establish persistent infections.
  • Host genetic and immune factors strongly influence tumorigenesis.
  • Virus infections are more common than virus-related tumors, so viruses are seldom complete carcinogens.
  • There are usually long latent periods between infection and tumor appearance.
  • Viral strains can differ in oncogenic potential.
  • Viruses can act directly, such as by integrating into the host genome and driving uncontrolled growth, or indirectly, such as by chronic inflammation and tissue damage.
  • Oncogenic viruses disrupt growth-control pathways.
  • Viral markers are usually present in tumor cells as evidence of viral contribution.
  • One virus may be linked to more than one tumor, as illustrated by HPV and both oropharyngeal and cervical cancers.
Central ideaViruses are often necessary but not sufficient.
Other mutations and host factors are commonly required before cancer fully develops.

Multistep viral carcinogenesis p. 7

  • Malignant transformation is a multistep process rather than an overnight event.
  • Intermediate cellular states include immortalized, hyperplastic, and preneoplastic cells.
  • Stepwise evolution involves cellular instability, accumulation of mutations, natural selection, and expansion of cells with a growth advantage.
  • Oncogene activation and tumor suppressor inactivation are central regardless of whether a virus is involved.
  • A tumor virus typically acts as a cofactor and may provide a few critical steps toward malignancy.

Persistent infection creates a long-term background for genetic instability and malignant transformation.

Molecular mechanisms p. 7

Cellular oncogenes versus tumor suppressor genes
FeatureCellular oncogenes / proto-oncogenesTumor suppressor genes
Normal roleRegulate cell growth, proliferation, division, differentiation, and genome integrity.Negative regulators of cell growth.
Cancer roleMutation or overexpression creates oncogenes that drive uncontrolled proliferation.Loss or inactivation removes growth restraint.
MechanismIncorrect expression or overproduction disrupts normal regulation. Viral promoter insertion can enhance gene expression.Both alleles must be inactivated for tumor formation in the lecture framework.
Examples—Rb prevents entry into S phase.
p53 halts the cell cycle or induces apoptosis after DNA damage and is described as mutated in 50% of human cancers.
Checkpoint
Activation of proto-oncogenes into oncogenes drives uncontrolled growth.
Loss of Rb or p53 removes important brakes on the cell cycle and apoptosis.

Persistent infection creates a long window for rare transforming events. When host immune control is weak, infected or transformed cells are more likely to grow unchecked. The lecture highlights immunosuppressed transplant recipients and people with HIV as examples at higher risk of EBV-associated lymphomas and HPV-related cancers.

RNA Tumor Viruses

Hepatitis C virus p. 8

  • Family: Flaviviridae.
  • Single-stranded RNA.
  • Chronic infection can progress to long-term inflammation and liver cirrhosis.
  • This background makes HCV a major causative factor for hepatocellular carcinoma.
  • The lecture states roughly 70 million chronic carriers globally and about 1–5% may develop hepatocellular carcinoma.

Retroviruses — important properties pp. 8–9

  • Most RNA tumor viruses in this lecture belong to the retrovirus family.
  • They carry an RNA-directed DNA polymerase, reverse transcriptase, which makes a DNA copy of viral RNA.
  • The DNA copy becomes a provirus integrated into host DNA.
  • Highly oncogenic or direct-transforming retroviruses carry their own oncogene and can push a cell toward cancer quickly.
  • Weakly oncogenic or slowly transforming retroviruses do not carry an oncogene and act indirectly, often over years.
Retrovirus structural properties
FeatureLecture description
VirionSpherical, 80–110 nm, helical nucleoprotein core within an icosahedral capsid.
CompositionRNA about 2%, protein about 60%, lipid about 35%, carbohydrate about 3%.
GenomePositive-sense ssRNA, linear, 7–11 kb, diploid with two copies.
ProteinReverse transcriptase is contained inside the virion.
EnvelopePresent.
ReplicationReverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA. DNA integrates into host chromosome as a provirus. The integrated provirus is used to produce new viral RNA and proteins.
MaturationVirions bud from the plasma membrane.
Cell effectRetroviral infections usually do not kill host cells. Lentiviruses are the stated exception and may be cytolytic.
Morphologic classification by electron microscopy
TypeMorphology
AIntracellular and noninfectious.
BEccentric nucleoid.
CLargest group of retroviruses. Nucleoids centrally located.

Retroviridae genera emphasized in the lecture
GenusExamples or characteristics
AlpharetrovirusAvian leukosis and sarcoma viruses.
BetaretrovirusMouse mammary tumor virus.
GammaretrovirusMammalian leukemia and sarcoma viruses.
DeltaretrovirusHuman T-lymphotropic viruses and bovine leukemia virus.

LentivirusSlow chronic infections, including HIV.
Host-of-origin patternRetroviruses occur in almost all vertebrates. Viruses from the same host share core-protein antigens, and cross-species infection is described as occasional.

Exogenous, endogenous, host range, and genes p. 9

Exogenous versus endogenous retroviruses
FeatureExogenousEndogenous
TransmissionSpread horizontally.Constant part of the genes of an organism and can be inherited.
BehaviorInitiate infection and possible transformation only after contact and entry.Usually silent and under host genetic control, but can be triggered to replicate.
LocationGene sequences are found only in infected cells.Found in all cells after germ-line integration.
NatureIncludes all pathogenic retroviruses such as HIV and HTLV.Usually not pathogenic.

Host range

  • A specific cell-surface receptor is a major determinant of retroviral host range.
  • Ecotropic viruses are highly species specific.
  • Amphotropic viruses have a broad host range.
  • Xenotropic viruses can replicate in some foreign-species cells but not in cultured cells from their natural host.

Core genetic content

  • gag — core proteins.
  • pro — protease.
  • pol — reverse transcriptase.
  • env — envelope glycoproteins.
  • Human deltaretroviruses and lentiviruses may carry additional downstream regulatory genes such as tax or tat.

General life cycle of retroviruses p. 9

Attachment. Viral proteins bind receptor and coreceptor. HIV example: CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4.
↓
Fusion and core release. The capsid core enters the cytoplasm and traffics toward nuclear pores.
↓
Uncoating and reverse transcription. A double-stranded DNA copy of the viral genome is produced.
↓
Integration. Integrase inserts viral DNA into the host genome as a provirus.
↓
Transcription. Host machinery transcribes the provirus into genomic RNA and mRNAs.
↓
Translation. Viral proteins are synthesized. Env proteins enter the ER membrane.
↓
Assembly. Viral RNA and proteins gather at the plasma membrane.
↓
Budding. Immature particles bud from the cell.
↓
Maturation. Viral protease cleaves Gag, producing a fully infectious virion.

Human T-lymphotropic virus and HIV as a cancer cofactor p. 9

HTLV-1

  • Causative agent of adult T-cell leukemia-lymphoma.
  • Has marked affinity for mature T cells.
  • Does not carry an oncogene.
  • LTR promoter and enhancer sequences respond to T-cell activation and proliferation.
  • TAX gene alters expression of viral and cellular genes, supporting replication and potentially disrupting growth regulation.
  • Lecture estimate: about 20 million people infected worldwide.
  • Main transmission: breastfeeding, blood transfusion, blood-contaminated needles, and sexual intercourse.
  • Early-life infections carry the highest later risk of ATL.

HIV

  • HIV is described as cytolytic and non-transforming.
  • It does not directly transform normal cells into cancer cells.
  • HIV-associated cancers are indirect, mainly through immune suppression.
  • Lecture examples include cervical cancer, Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas, head and neck cancers, liver cancer, and oral cavity cancer.

Hepatitis B virus p. 10

  • Hepadnaviridae.
  • 42 nm spherical enveloped virus.
  • Circular double-stranded DNA genome.
  • Important risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma.
  • Most adult infections resolve, while neonatal and early-childhood infection is much more likely to become chronic, up to 90% in the lecture.
  • Persistent infection established early in life gives the highest later HCC risk.
  • Lecture pathway: persistent infection → necrosis → inflammation → liver regeneration → cirrhosis → HCC background.
  • HBx or X protein acts as a potential viral oncoprotein.
  • Aflatoxin may act together with HBV to increase HCC risk.
  • More than 250 million people were described as chronically infected, with over 800,000 deaths yearly from complications.
  • HBV vaccine prevents infection and significantly reduces HCC risk.

Polyomaviruses pp. 10–11

Important properties
FeatureLecture description
VirionSmall icosahedral particle, about 45 nm.
GenomeCircular double-stranded DNA, about 5 kbp.
ProteinsThree structural proteins. Cellular histones condense DNA in the virion.
EnvelopeNone.
ReplicationNucleus.
  • Early region encodes T antigens that regulate replication and can transform host cells.
  • Late region encodes structural coat proteins, which are not required for transformation and may be absent in transformed cells.
  • SV40 large T antigen binds p53 and retinoblastoma-family proteins, forcing S-phase entry and weakening DNA-damage responses.

VirionIcosahedral, about 55 nm.
GenomeCircular dsDNA, about 8 kbp.
ProteinsTwo structural proteins. Cellular histones condense viral DNA.
EnvelopeNone.

Classification and epidemiology
Papillomaviridae is described as a very large family, formerly grouped in Papovaviridae.
The lecture states 16 genera overall, with five genera infecting humans: Alpha-, Beta-, Gamma-, Mupa-, and Nupapillomavirus.
Genital HPV is described as the most common viral infection of the reproductive tract, with a peak in adolescents and young adults under 25 years.
Immunocompromised patients, men who have sex with men, and individuals with HIV are highlighted as higher-risk groups.
Women under 20 years are not routinely tested in the lecture because early HPV infections often clear spontaneously.
Attachment. HPV docks to extracellular matrix or basement membrane through heparan sulfate proteoglycans. Host enzymes reshape the particle and help move it toward entry sites.
↓
Entry. Mainly endocytosis with actin remodeling and movement to early endosomes.
↓
Early endosome. CD63 and RAB5 help maintain early-endosome localization. Acidification begins capsid disassembly and links viral DNA with L2.
↓
Uncoating and trafficking. Secretase cleaves L2. L2 recruits the retromer complex. RAB proteins guide the DNA-L2 complex toward the trans-Golgi network.
↓
Transport to nucleus. DNA-L2 travels along microtubules. During mitosis it accesses the nucleus and PML nuclear bodies.
↓
Replication and persistence. Early proteins such as E2 help tether viral DNA to host chromosomes, maintaining episomal DNA through cell divisions.
HPV type associations
TypesLecture association
1, 2, 4, 7Benign warts.
5, 8Epidermodysplasia verruciformis with occasional progression to cancer.
6, 11Low-risk mucosal types causing most genital warts and laryngeal papillomas.
16, 18High-risk types with strongest association with cervical cancer and other cancers.
31, 33, 45, 56High risk but more moderate cancer correlation than 16 and 18 in the lecture.
  • HPV 16 and 18 together cause more than 70% of cervical cancer, with HPV 16 described as most common.
  • HPV is the established cause of more than 99% of cervical cancers and more than 80% of anal cancers in the lecture.
  • Persistent high-risk infection is a necessary component of carcinoma development.
  • Most infections clear within 2–3 years. The problem is persistence.
  • Low-risk HPV 6 and 11 cause about 90% of anogenital warts and can cause childhood laryngeal papillomas.

Prevention

  • Pap smear screening detects precancerous change before progression.
  • HPV testing by DNA hybridization or PCR improves screening sensitivity and specificity.
  • Vaccines listed: bivalent HPV 16 and 18, quadrivalent HPV 6, 11, 16, and 18, and 9-valent HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58.
  • Vaccines are not therapeutic for established HPV disease.
  • Lecture states immunity lasts at least 10 years.

Herpesviruses and oncogenesis p. 12

  • Large enveloped dsDNA viruses with icosahedral capsids.
  • Size given as about 125–200 nm, with genomes around 125–240 kbp.
  • Typical pattern: acute infection → latency → lifelong recurrence.
  • Several human herpesviruses are associated with tumors.

Epstein-Barr virus

  • Infects B lymphocytes and causes infectious mononucleosis.
  • Can immortalize B lymphocytes, allowing indefinite growth in culture.
  • Associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin disease, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders.
  • In immunosuppressed transplant patients, the lecture notes that post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease can be detected early through blood screening for EBV DNA.
  • LMP1 acts like a constantly active growth-factor receptor and is important in B-cell transformation.
  • EBNAs support B-cell immortalization.
  • EBNA1 is the only protein consistently expressed in Burkitt lymphoma cells in the lecture and can interfere with antigen processing to help immune evasion.

HHV-8 / KSHV

  • Associated with Kaposi sarcoma.
  • Also linked to primary effusion lymphoma and Multicentric Castleman disease.

HIV — Foundations, Structure & Biology

Introduction and classification pp. 12–13

  • HIV is a lentivirus and the cause of AIDS.
  • First recognized and described by 1981. HIV-1 was isolated in 1983.
  • Infection is lifelong.
  • Without treatment, most patients develop fatal opportunistic infections within about a decade.
  • HAART transformed HIV from a fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition.
HIV-1 versus HIV-2
HIV-1HIV-2
Responsible for the global pandemic.
Groups M, N, and O.
Group M contains multiple subtypes and recombinant forms.
Linked in the lecture to chimpanzees.		Found mainly in West Africa.
Further divided into eight subtypes, A through H.
Linked in the lecture to sooty mangabeys.
Genome variabilityStructural genes gag and pol are highly conserved, while envelope glycoproteins show extensive variability that complicates vaccine development.

Properties of lentiviruses p. 13

FeatureLecture description
VirionSpherical, 80–100 nm, with a distinctive cylindrical core.

EnvelopePresent.

Study aidCylindrical core + lentivirus + slow chronic disease is the lecture’s structural and biologic anchor for HIV.

Natural disease pattern and receptors pp. 13–14

  • Spread mainly by exchange of body fluids.
  • Persists lifelong, often at low levels.
  • Hallmark: high mutation rates and formation of quasispecies.
  • Macrophages and monocytes can transport hidden virus through the body and are described as a Trojan horse.
  • Lymphocyte-tropic strains produce highly productive infection. Macrophage-tropic strains show more restricted replication.
  • Long incubation can last months to years.
  • Antibodies form but do not eliminate the virus.
HIV receptors and coreceptors
MoleculeLecture role
CD4First receptor. Expressed on lymphocytes and macrophages.
CCR5Main coreceptor for macrophage-tropic strains. CCR5 mutations may confer natural resistance or delayed progression. This discovery led to an entry inhibitor.
CXCR4Main coreceptor for lymphocyte-tropic strains.
α4β7 integrinHelps HIV infection in the gut.
DC-SIGNDoes not directly mediate entry in the lecture. It transports HIV to lymphoid tissues and enhances T-cell infection.
Host factors influencing pathogenesisAge, stress, genetics, and concurrent infections can accelerate disease or increase transmission risks.

HIV — Epidemiology & Routes of Transmission

Global burden p. 14

40.8 M
Estimated people living with HIV worldwide by end of 2024.
1.3 M
Estimated new HIV infections in 2024.
630,000
Estimated HIV-related deaths in 2024.
91.4 M
People stated to have acquired HIV since the epidemic began.
  • Of the 40.8 million living with HIV: about 1.4 million children aged 0–14 and 39.4 million adults over 15.
  • New infections declined about 40% from 2.2 million in 2010 to 1.3 million in 2024.
  • About 120,000 of new infections in 2024 were children and 1.2 million were adults.
  • HIV-related mortality fell about 54% from 2010 and about 70% from the 2004 peak.
  • More than 44 million deaths since the epidemic began are cited in the lecture.
  • WHO framing in the lecture: 90% of new infections each year occur in developing countries, with predominantly heterosexual transmission and roughly equal numbers of men and women.

Factors driving global spread and Philippine lecture data p. 14

  • Urban migration from rural areas.
  • International travel for tourism and business.
  • Civil unrest and displacement.
Philippines data as presented in the lecture
The lecture describes the Philippines as having the fastest-growing HIV epidemic in the Western Pacific Region.
It cites 418% change in new HIV infections and 535% change in AIDS-related deaths from 2010 to 2022.
As of March 2024, DOH was stated to report about 55 new diagnoses per day.
Of 122,255 people living with HIV, 64% or 78,633 were stated to be on ART.
A projection is given from an estimated 189,000 PLHIV at end of 2023 to 401,700 by 2030.

Routes of transmission p. 15

Sexual transmission

  • High-viral-load fluids highlighted: blood and semen.
  • Sexual contact includes genital-oral sex.
  • Risk can increase up to 100-fold with other STDs such as syphilis, gonorrhea, or HSV-2 because inflammation and ulcers facilitate mucosal entry.
  • Risk increases with multiple partners.
  • Asymptomatic individuals can still transmit HIV.

Parenteral exposure

  • Contaminated blood products and shared injection needles.
  • In the early epidemic, over 90% of hemophiliacs receiving contaminated clotting factor were stated to develop HIV.
  • Current transfusion risk in the lecture is reduced to <1 in 1 million because of donor screening and testing.

Mother-to-child

  • In utero, during delivery, or through breastfeeding.
  • Untreated transmission rate: 13–40%.
  • One-third to one-half of perinatal infections in Africa were linked to breastfeeding, usually within the first six months.
  • Higher maternal viral load means higher risk.

Occupational exposure

ExposureRisk in lecture
Needlestick<0.3%
Mucous membraneAbout 0.09%
ComparisonHepatitis C around 1.8% and hepatitis B around 6–30% are cited as higher.

HIV — Pathogenesis, Pathology & Clinical Findings

Natural course of untreated HIV pp. 15–16

The lecture presents HIV as a continuous process rather than a truly dormant infection. Viral load, CD4 count, and the site of active replication change across the stages.

1. Primary infection
Mucosal entry → initial viremia → dissemination to lymphoid organs → acute illness → sharp CD4 fall.
↓
2. Immune response
Plasma viremia falls and CD4 cells partially rebound, but HIV is not eliminated and persists in lymph nodes.
↓
3. Clinical latency
The patient may appear healthy, yet HIV remains biologically active with continued replication in lymphoid tissues and progressive CD4 loss.
↓
4. Constitutional symptoms
Falling CD4 counts are accompanied by weight loss, fever, night sweats, and other clinical manifestations.
↓
5. Late stage / AIDS
Viral load rises again, CD4 cells become severely depleted, and life-threatening opportunistic disease develops.
Stage-by-stage pathophysiology
StageTiming / viral activityCD4 patternWhat is happening
Primary infectionInitial viremia reaches blood in about 4–11 days.
Viremia can remain detectable for 8–12 weeks.
Acute phase occurs around 3–6 weeks.		Sharp fallRapid replication and wide dissemination seed lymphoid organs.
A mononucleosis-like illness occurs in about 50–75%.
Immune responseAbout 1 week to 3 months after infection.Partial reboundImmune control lowers plasma viremia, but the virus remains in lymph nodes because it is not completely eliminated.
Clinical latencyAverage untreated progression is about 10 years.Below normal, then gradually declinesLatency is not viral inactivity.
The lecture describes ongoing high-level turnover with about 10 billion HIV particles produced and destroyed daily.
Once infected, CD4 T cells have an average half-life of about 1.6 days.
Advanced diseaseViral expression and plasma viral load increase.Progressive depletionConstitutional symptoms, opportunistic infections, neoplasms, and other manifestations appear.
Untreated late stageThe lecture states death usually occurs within about 2 years after symptom onset.Nearly depleted in late stageFull-blown AIDS develops with severe immunosuppression and life-threatening opportunistic disease.

Why HIV persists and why CD4 cells fall p. 15

CD4 T lymphocytes

  • CD4 is the primary receptor for the HIV envelope.
    • CD4 T-cell depletion is a central feature and the hallmark of HIV infection.
    • CD4 T cells coordinate the immune response by acting on macrophages, cytotoxic T cells, NK cells, and B cells.
  • How CD4 cells are lost
    • Direct killing from viral replication.
    • Indirect death of uninfected T cells.
  • Tropism changes with progression
    • Early infection is dominated by M-tropic strains that target macrophages and CD4 T cells.
    • As disease progresses, there is a shift toward T-tropic strains that infect CD4 T cells more efficiently.
    • CCR5 is the major coreceptor for macrophage-tropic strains.
    • CXCR4 is the major coreceptor for lymphocyte-tropic strains.

Memory CD4 cells and the latent reservoir

  • Not every infected CD4 cell dies.
    • Some infected cells return to a resting memory state.
    • These cells may contain provirus without actively producing virus.
    • They can persist for decades, which is a major reason standard therapy does not cure HIV.
  • During successful ART, fewer than 1 per million CD4 T cells may harbor provirus.
    • The reservoir declines extremely slowly.
    • The lecture estimates natural clearance could take up to 70 years.
  • Reactivation can occur after antigen exposure or after stopping ART.
  • Other possible reservoirs listed in the lecture include macrophages, HSCs, and brain cells.
Lecture example
Berlin patient, 2007: cited as a functional cure after a bone marrow transplant from a donor with a CCR5 mutation.
The example emphasizes the importance of CCR5 in HIV entry and persistence.
Cells and tissues that sustain HIV infection
Site / cellEntry or rolePathophysiologic importance
CD4 T lymphocytesCD4 receptor with a coreceptorMain virus producers.
Progressive depletion weakens coordinated cellular and humoral immune responses.
Monocytes / macrophagesCD4 with CCR5Central to early spread.
Resist HIV cytopathic effects, can act as reservoirs, and provide long-term virus production.
Transport HIV to organs including the lungs and brain.
Brain-associated macrophage lineage cellsMajor targets of infection in the brainContribute to the lecture-described neuropsychiatric manifestations.
Lymphoid organsContain the majority of lymphocytesThe lecture calls them the heart of HIV infection.

Cause-and-effect chain
Cytokines activate CD4 T cells → activated cells become more susceptible to infection.
Ongoing replication + CD4 loss + progressive destruction of lymph-node architecture → progressively weaker immune responses.

Viral evolution and progression to AIDS p. 15

  • Early infection
    • Usually a single viral variant establishes infection.
    • The early viral population is relatively homogeneous.
  • Ongoing replication
    • Rapid replication plus error-prone reverse transcriptase generates accumulating quasispecies.
  • Progression
    • Constitutional symptoms and clinical disease appear.
    • Opportunistic infections and neoplasms emerge as immune function declines.
    • Plasma viral load increases in the advanced stage.
    • Late-stage strains become more virulent and cytopathic.
  • Typical tropism shift
    • M-tropic monocyte or macrophage strains dominate early.
    • A shift toward T-tropic lymphocyte strains accompanies progression toward full-blown AIDS.

Clinical findings through the disease course p. 16

Clinical phase / markerLecture-supported findings
Acute HIV infectionNonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, rash, headache, nausea, and night sweats.
Prodrome before full-blown AIDSThe lecture uses the phrase “diarrhea & dwindling”.
Fatigue, malaise, weight loss, fever, shortness of breath, chronic diarrhea, hairy leukoplakia, candidiasis, and lymphadenopathy.
AIDSHallmark is severe immunosuppression with opportunistic infections and cancers such as Kaposi sarcoma.
GI involvementMajor cause of debility.
Untreated timelineAbout 8–10 years before symptoms appear, followed by AIDS and death in about 2 years without treatment.
Plasma viral load
Viral load reflects the balance between viral replication and cell killing.
The steady-state level reached by an individual is the viral set point.
High set point → faster progression and poorer treatment response.
Viral load is the best predictor of long-term outcome.
CD4 count is used to estimate the short-term risk of opportunistic disease.
Viral RNA measurements are also used to monitor antiretroviral therapy.

Neurologic disease

  • Neurologic disease is described in 40–90% of patients.
    • Subacute encephalitis
    • Vacuolar myelopathy
    • Aseptic meningitis
    • Peripheral neuropathy
  • AIDS-dementia complex is listed as the most common neurologic syndrome.
    • Late-stage disorder affecting up to 65% of AIDS patients in the lecture.
    • Memory loss, poor concentration, apathy, and behavioral changes.
    • Average survival stated as <6 months.

Pediatric AIDS

  • Acquisition and course
    • Perinatal transmission is typically acquired from infected mothers during birth.
    • Without treatment, symptoms may appear before age two and death may follow about two years later.
    • High plasma viral load predicts more rapid progression than in adults.
  • Clinical findings
    • Interstitial pneumonitis and pneumonia.
    • Severe oral candidiasis.
    • Encephalopathy.
    • Stunting, wasting, and growth retardation.
    • Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.
    • Sepsis and diarrhea.
  • Neurologic / psychiatric findings
    • Seizures, developmental delay, encephalopathy, bacterial meningitis, and psychiatric risk.
    • The lecture notes that children now live longer because of ART and that anxiety disorders are increasingly recognized.

HIV — Laboratory Diagnosis, Treatment & Control

Plasma viral load and laboratory diagnosis pp. 16–17

High-yield markers
Viral load is the best predictor of long-term outcome and progression.
CD4 count estimates short-term risk of opportunistic disease.
A patient’s steady-state viral level is the viral set point. Higher set point predicts faster progression and poorer treatment response.
Diagnostic approaches
MethodLecture details
Virus isolationHIV can be cultured from peripheral-blood lymphocytes. Most sensitive method is coculture with uninfected mitogen-stimulated cells. Growth is confirmed by reverse transcriptase activity or p24 after 1–2 weeks. Slow and labor-intensive, mainly research use.
SerologyBackbone of testing. EIA/ELISA sensitivity stated as >98%.
Traditional Western blot required two reactive bands among p24, gp41, or gp120/gp160, but the lecture notes WHO and CDC have phased this out in favor of HIV RNA testing or newer fourth-generation assays.
Rapid antibody tests can use blood or oral fluid.
SeroconversionUsually around 3–4 weeks, with nearly all positive by six months.
PCR / NATRT-PCR, DNA PCR, and branched-DNA assays detect HIV RNA or DNA directly. They can detect infection before seroconversion.
Early infant diagnosisRNA/DNA PCR is the gold standard because maternal antibody interferes with serologic testing.
p24 antigenEarly marker detectable before antibodies. Disappears after seroconversion or after antibody-antigen complexing. Reappearance later suggests poor prognosis.
Fourth generationHIV antibody plus p24 antigen, shortening the diagnostic window.
Fifth generationCan simultaneously differentiate HIV-1 antibody, HIV-2 antibody, and p24 antigen.

Resistance testing p. 17

  • Essential to guide therapy.
  • Genotypic testing is the standard and most common method.
  • It sequences reverse transcriptase and protease genes to detect resistance mutations.
  • Results are interpreted using expert databases such as those maintained by the International AIDS Society.
  • Phenotypic testing grows recombinant virus with drugs and measures drug concentrations required to inhibit replication. It is less common and useful for complex mutation patterns.
  • Clinical use: at diagnosis and whenever treatment failure occurs.
  • Other assays can examine integrase resistance, fusion-inhibitor resistance, or coreceptor tropism for CCR5 antagonists.

Antiviral drug classes p. 17

ClassMechanismDrugs listed in lecture
Reverse transcriptase inhibitorsBlock viral RNA-to-DNA conversion. Includes nucleoside or nucleotide agents and NNRTIs.Nucleoside / nucleotide: Abacavir, Didanosine, Emtricitabine, Lamivudine, Stavudine, Tenofovir, Zidovudine.
Nonnucleoside: Delavirdine, Efavirenz, Etravirine, Nevirapine, Rilpivirine.
Protease inhibitorsBlock essential viral protease and prevent maturation into infectious particles.Atazanavir, Darunavir, Fosamprenavir, Indinavir, Nelfinavir, Ritonavir, Saquinavir, Tipranavir.
Fusion inhibitorPrevents viral entry.Enfuvirtide.
Entry inhibitorBlocks CCR5 binding and prevents HIV entry.Maraviroc.
Integrase inhibitorsPrevent chromosomal integration of viral DNA into host chromosomes.Dolutegravir, Raltegravir.

HAART, treatment challenges, and prevention p. 17

HAART

  • Introduced in 1996 in the lecture.
  • Uses a combination of drugs and transformed HIV into a manageable chronic disease.
  • Suppresses viral replication to an undetectable plasma viral load.
  • Restores immune response and prolongs survival.
  • Does not cure HIV because latent viral reservoirs persist.
  • Monotherapy quickly leads to resistance.
  • Combination therapy delays resistance, although cross-resistance within drug classes can occur.

Challenges

  • Drug resistance is increasing and can be present even in newly diagnosed patients.
  • Lecture example: about 19% resistant strains among perinatally infected infants.
  • Drugs are expensive, lifelong, and can have side effects such as lipodystrophy.
  • Limited access remains a problem in many parts of the world.
  • Breastfeeding transmission remains a challenge.

Prevention role

  • PrEP significantly reduces infection risk.
  • Zidovudine or AZT can reduce mother-to-child transmission by up to 70% in the lecture.
  • Shorter AZT or nevirapine regimens are noted for resource-limited settings.
  • Safe and effective vaccines are described as the best hope for global control, but candidate vaccines have been ineffective or only partially effective.
  • Challenges include rapid HIV mutation, high env variability, incomplete immune clearance, and unknown correlates of protective immunity.
  • Vaccine work is also hindered by animal-model limitations. The lecture notes that chimpanzees do not develop AIDS after infection, while macaques are useful but imperfect substitutes.

Patient education

  • Adherence to ART is the most important point.
  • Routine viral-load and CD4 monitoring.
  • Prevent transmission through safe sex and avoiding needle sharing.
  • Healthy lifestyle with nutrition, exercise, and mental-health support.
  • Vaccines and prophylaxis against opportunistic infections.
  • Counseling, peer support, stigma reduction, and quality-of-life support.

Fast final review, reorganized into tables, nested recall cues, and cause-and-effect chains. Details remain lecture-grounded.

Rabies — identity, replication, and spread pp. 1–5

AnchorMust remember
IdentityRhabdoviridae → Lyssavirus.
Rod or bullet shaped, enveloped, nonsegmented −ssRNA.

N mRNA is most abundant.
L mRNA is least abundant.

NeuroinvasionBite / scratch → local site and muscle → nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction → retrograde axonal transport → CNS → centrifugal spread to other tissues and salivary glands.
Spread trapNo well-documented hematogenous spread is described.

Eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion in neurons, especially Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal neurons.

Hydrophobia and excitability are absent. Commonly confused with Guillain-Barré syndrome.
  • Diagnosis
    • The lecture states there is no test that diagnoses rabies before clinical symptoms appear.
    • After symptoms begin, confirmation can use immunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase detection, RT-PCR, serology, viral isolation, and pathology.
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis
    • Category 1: wash exposed skin. No vaccine or RIG.
    • Category 2: wash wound and start vaccine. No RIG.
    • Category 3: wash wound and give vaccine + RIG immediately.
    • All Category II exposures on the head and neck are managed as Category III.
  • Pre-exposure prophylaxis
    • Immunologically naive schedule: day 0 and 7.
    • Lecture options: 2-site ID or 1-site IM administration.

Human cancer viruses — the association map pp. 6–12

Core concept
Viral carcinogenesis is a multistep process.
Virus infection is more common than virus-related tumor formation.
Tumor viruses are seldom complete carcinogens by themselves.
Long latent periods often separate initial infection from tumor appearance.
VirusMechanism / defining pointMajor association
HTLV-1TAX alters viral and cellular gene expression.Adult T-cell leukemia / lymphoma
HCVChronic infection, inflammation, and cirrhosis create the background for carcinogenesis.Hepatocellular carcinoma
HBVPersistent infection with chronic injury and regeneration.
HBV X protein is presented as a potential oncoprotein.		Hepatocellular carcinoma
HPV 16 and 18Persistent high-risk HPV infection is necessary for carcinoma development.
E6 → p53.
E7 → pRb.		Cervical and other anogenital cancers, with HPV 16 also important in oropharyngeal cancer
HPV 6 and 11Low-risk mucosal types.Most genital warts and laryngeal papillomas

HIV — identity, receptors, genes, and replication pp. 12–14

FeatureHigh-yield recall
ClassificationRetroviridae → Lentivirus.
HIV is the cause of AIDS.
VirionSpherical, 80–100 nm, with a distinctive cylindrical core.
GenomeLinear positive-sense ssRNA, 9–10 kb, diploid.
Core genesgag = core proteins.
pro = protease.
pol = reverse transcriptase.
env = envelope proteins.
Replication anchorGenomic RNA → reverse transcriptase makes DNA → viral DNA integrates permanently as a provirus → proviral DNA templates viral RNA → particles bud from the plasma membrane and mature.
Genetic diversityHigh viral replication rate + high reverse-transcriptase error rate → quasispecies.
Envelope glycoproteins show extensive variability.
Envelope proteins and receptors
ComponentFunction
gp120Binds CD4 and a coreceptor.
Determines lymphocyte versus macrophage tropism.
Contains major antigenic sites and five variable regions, with V3 important for neutralization.
gp41Anchors the envelope protein and provides the fusion domain that mediates entry.
CCR5Main coreceptor for M-tropic strains.
CCR5 mutations may confer natural resistance or delayed progression.
CXCR4Main coreceptor for T-tropic strains.
α4β7 integrinHelps HIV infection in the gut.
DC-SIGNDoes not directly mediate entry in the lecture.
Transports HIV to lymphoid tissue and enhances T-cell infection.
Six accessory genes
GeneFunction
TatBoosts transcription.
RevExports unspliced viral RNA from the nucleus for late structural-protein production.
NefIncreases infectivity and decreases CD4 and MHC-I.
VprNuclear transport and G2 arrest.
VpuAccelerates CD4 degradation.
VifBlocks the antiviral restriction factor APOBEC3G.

HIV — pathogenesis and clinical progression pp. 15–16

StageViral loadCD4Exam-ready cue
Primary infectionRapid riseSharp fallBloodstream in 4–11 days.
Acute phase around 3–6 weeks.
Mononucleosis-like illness in 50–75%.
Immune responseDeclinesPartial reboundAbout 1 week to 3 months.
Virus persists in lymph nodes.
Clinical latencyLower than acute phase but ongoingSlow progressive declineNot true viral inactivity.
About 10 billion HIV particles produced / destroyed daily in the lecture.
Constitutional phaseIncreasingFallingWeight loss, fever, night sweats, and other symptoms.
AIDSSurgesNearly depletedSevere immunosuppression, opportunistic infections, and neoplasms.
  • Persistent reservoir
    • Resting memory CD4 cells can harbor latent provirus for decades.
    • On ART, fewer than 1 per million CD4 T cells may harbor provirus.
    • The lecture estimates natural clearance of the reservoir could take up to 70 years.
    • Reactivation can occur after antigen exposure or stopping ART.
  • Macrophages
    • Use CD4 plus CCR5.
    • Important in early spread, long-term production, and transport to lungs and brain.
    • Act as reservoirs and are relatively resistant to HIV cytopathic effects.
  • Lymphoid tissue
    • Contains most lymphocytes and is the heart of HIV infection.
    • Only about 2% of lymphocytes are found in blood.
    • HIV continues active replication there even during clinical latency.
  • Progression cue
    • Early: M-tropic / CCR5.
    • Later: shift toward T-tropic / CXCR4.
    • Advanced disease: plasma viral load rises and late strains become more virulent and cytopathic.
Markers to separate
Viral load = best predictor of long-term progression.
Viral set point = steady-state viral level. Higher set point predicts faster progression and poorer treatment response.
CD4 count = estimates short-term risk of opportunistic disease.
CD4 <200 cells/μL = opportunistic infections become a major late-stage concern in the lecture.

HIV — transmission, diagnosis, and treatment pp. 15–17

Transmission anchors
RouteLecture cue
SexualBlood and semen are major high-viral-load fluids.
Other STDs with inflammation or ulcers can increase risk dramatically, stated as up to 100-fold.
ParenteralShared needles and contaminated blood products.
Current transfusion risk stated as <1 in 1 million after donor screening and testing.
Mother to childIn utero, during delivery, or breastfeeding.
Untreated maternal transmission rate stated as 13–40%.
Higher maternal viral load increases risk.
OccupationalNeedlestick risk <0.3%.
Mucous-membrane exposure about 0.09%.
Diagnostic marker matrix
Marker / testWhat to remember
EIA / ELISABackbone of serologic testing.
Lecture sensitivity stated as >98%.
SeroconversionUsually around 3–4 weeks, with nearly all positive by six months.
p24 antigenEarly marker before antibodies.
Disappears after seroconversion or antibody-antigen complexing.
Reappearance later suggests poor prognosis.
4th generationHIV antibody + p24 antigen.
5th generationDifferentiates HIV-1 antibody, HIV-2 antibody, and p24 antigen.
PCR / NATRT-PCR, DNA PCR, and bDNA assays directly detect viral nucleic acid and can detect infection before seroconversion.
Early infant diagnosisRNA/DNA PCR is the gold standard in the lecture because maternal antibodies interfere with serologic testing.
Resistance testingGenotypic testing is the standard and most common method.
Phenotypic testing is less common and is useful for complex mutation patterns.
Antiretroviral classes
ClassMain targetLecture examples
Reverse transcriptase inhibitorsBlock RNA → DNA conversionTenofovir, Zidovudine, Efavirenz, and others listed in the lecture
Protease inhibitorsPrevent maturation into infectious particlesRitonavir, Darunavir, and others listed in the lecture
Fusion inhibitorPrevents viral entryEnfuvirtide
Entry inhibitorBlocks CCR5 bindingMaraviroc
Integrase inhibitorsPrevent chromosomal integration of viral DNADolutegravir, Raltegravir
  • HAART
    • Introduced in 1996 in the lecture.
    • Combination therapy suppresses viral replication to an undetectable plasma viral load, restores immune response, and prolongs survival.
    • It does not cure HIV because latent reservoirs persist.
    • Monotherapy quickly leads to resistance. Combination therapy delays resistance.
  • Prevention
    • PrEP significantly reduces infection risk.
    • AZT can reduce mother-to-child transmission by up to 70% in the lecture.
    • Vaccine development is difficult because HIV mutates rapidly, env is highly variable, infection is not fully cleared by immunity, and correlates of protective immunity remain uncertain.
  • Most important patient-education point
    • Adherence to ART.
    • Routine viral-load and CD4 monitoring.
    • Safe sex and avoidance of needle sharing.
